profile.reading:
Meta's Richland Parish Data Center near Holly Ridge in northeast Louisiana houses Hyperion, which Meta calls its largest multi-gigawatt AI training cluster. Construction began in December 2024. On 13 July 2026 Meta said it was expanding the site to 5 GW of compute capacity, the largest in its fleet, with investment of more than $50 billion, up from an original design of about 2 GW.

Power comes through Entergy Louisiana. The Louisiana Public Service Commission approved three combined-cycle gas plants for the project in August 2025, and a revised agreement in 2026 adds seven more gas plants, grid-scale batteries at three sites and solar capacity. Meta says it pays the full cost of energy and related infrastructure.

The 5 GW figure is Meta's stated plan. Coordinates are from the site's Wikipedia entry, which cites Meta's data center page.

reading.body:
Meta's Richland Parish data center is planned at 5 GW of compute, roughly two and a half times its original 2 GW design, making power procurement the project's central fact.

The site is a 4 million square foot facility under construction in northeast Louisiana since December 2024, with more than $50 billion attached to the expansion Meta announced on 13 July 2026. The generation to serve it is being built alongside it: three combined-cycle gas plants approved by the Louisiana Public Service Commission in August 2025, then a revised 2026 agreement adding seven more gas plants, grid-scale batteries at three sites, and solar, all through Entergy Louisiana. That is the pattern worth noting. The compute capacity and the power supply are being expanded in the same documents, and the utility filing is where the real schedule lives.

For AI specifically, the 5 GW figure is a plan, not a measured load, and the data says so. It is Meta's stated compute capacity at full build. The first Entergy gas plants are not expected online until the end of 2028, which means the gap between announced compute and deliverable power is measured in years. A cluster of this size cannot train anything until the generation exists, and the generation is being permitted and built one plant at a time.

What this does not cover: there is no published IT capacity, which the suitability inputs list as missing, so the 5 GW cannot be checked against a metered or contracted number. The coordinates come from a Wikipedia entry citing Meta's own data center page, not from a survey. Nothing here reports actual electricity consumption, water use, or local grid conditions beyond the named plants.

suitability.basis: weighted mean of the published inputs named here, scaled to 100; formula on the methodology page
